name: Design a Durable Workflow Engine
intent: Run business processes that last days or months, written as ordinary code, so that they survive crashes, deploys and retries without losing a step or doing a step twice.
codeTitle: an event-sourced workflow with replay and idempotent activities
finalIntro: One order workflow surviving an activity crash and a workflow worker crash, then waiting days for a signal.
prompt: Design a platform on which teams write long-running processes such as order fulfilment or customer onboarding. A process calls other services in order, waits for people and timers for hours or months, and compensates when a later step fails. It must keep going when machines crash or new code is deployed, and it must run millions of processes at once.
functional: Start a workflow from code or an API, and give it a unique id
Run steps that call other systems (activities) with timeouts and automatic retries
Sleep for seconds or months with a durable timer
Send a signal to a running workflow, and query its current state
Undo earlier steps when a later one fails (compensation)
Show the full history of what every workflow did, and why it is waiting
Deploy new workflow code while old instances are still running
nonFunctional: No lost progress: a crash of any worker or node may delay a workflow but never reset it
Every activity runs at least once, and a business side effect happens once, through idempotency
Millions of open workflows and tens of thousands of state transitions per second
A worker crash is noticed and recovered within seconds, and a step starts within about 100 ms
Sleeping workflows cost almost nothing: no thread or memory is held while one waits
Bounded history per workflow, so replay stays fast
Strict isolation between teams, and an audit trail of every decision

firstAttempt.text: Write each process as one long script that runs in a single process: call the stock service, charge the card, ship, send the email, using sleep() to wait and try/catch with a loop for retries. The state lives in local variables. To survive a restart, save the order's status in a table after each step and let a cron job restart the unfinished ones.
limits: A crash loses every local variable, so the script cannot continue from where it was; the cron job can only start again from the top
Starting again repeats steps that already happened, such as charging the card a second time
A sleep of three days holds a process, and a deploy or restart in that time kills it
Retry loops, timeouts and the status table are rewritten, slightly differently, in every script
Nobody can see why order 7731 is stuck, because the story exists only in log lines
Changing the script while thousands of orders are in the middle of it has no safe answer

steps.title: Keep an append-only history of every decision and result
steps.problem: State in local variables and a status column cannot say what already happened, so after a crash nobody knows which steps ran.
steps.fix: Every workflow gets an id and a history: an append-only list of events such as 'workflow started', 'activity charge_card scheduled', 'activity charge_card completed with this result', 'timer started', 'signal received'. A workflow service accepts start and signal requests and only ever appends to the history. The state of a workflow at any moment is a fold over its events, which is event sourcing applied to the process itself. Each append is a single database transaction that also checks that the history has not changed under the writer, so two writers cannot both extend it.
steps.tradeoff: The history is a complete audit trail and the only source of truth, so there is nothing to get out of step. Reading the current state means reading the events, and the log grows with every step, which later needs a limit.

steps.title: Rebuild state by replaying deterministic code on any worker
steps.problem: The code of the process runs somewhere, and when that machine dies its local variables die with it, even though the history survived.
steps.fix: Workflow code is ordinary code, but it must be deterministic: no wall clock, no random numbers, no direct network calls, only calls to the engine. A workflow worker takes a decision task from a task queue, loads the history, and runs the code from the top. When the code calls an activity that already has a result in the history, the call returns that result at once. When it reaches a call with no result, the code stops, and the worker returns one command, for example 'schedule charge_card'. The service appends it, and the next decision task is queued. Any worker can do this, so a crash only means another worker replays the history. Workers pull tasks with a long poll, which means no scheduler pushes work to a dead machine. A worker keeps recently used workflows cached and the service prefers it for the next task of the same workflow (a sticky queue), which avoids a full replay in the common case.
steps.tradeoff: Crashes cost one replay, and workers are interchangeable and scale by adding more. The price is the determinism rule: code that reads the clock or iterates a map in random order can decide differently on replay and corrupts the workflow, so it must be caught by tests and checks.

steps.title: Run side effects as activities with timeouts, retries and heartbeats
steps.problem: Charging a card or reserving stock is a side effect that cannot be replayed, and the call can fail, hang or succeed with a lost reply.
steps.fix: Side effects live only in activities, which run on separate activity workers and are scheduled through their own task queue. Each activity has a start-to-close timeout, a schedule-to-close deadline, and a retry policy: initial interval, backoff multiplier, a maximum interval, a maximum number of attempts, and a list of errors that must not be retried. A long activity sends heartbeats, so a silent worker is declared dead after a few missed beats rather than after the full timeout, and the heartbeat can carry progress so the retry resumes from there. Delivery is at-least-once, because a retry cannot tell 'never ran' from 'ran but the reply was lost', so every activity passes an idempotency key (workflow id plus step) to the system it calls, and the other system returns the first result for a repeat.
steps.tradeoff: A flaky downstream service becomes a retry with backoff and not an incident, and a failed attempt is invisible to the workflow code. The engine cannot make an external effect exactly once by itself, so the idempotency key and the other system's cooperation carry the weight, and retries without limits can hammer a service that is already down.

steps.title: Add durable timers, signals and sagas that undo earlier steps
steps.problem: A real process waits for three days for a delivery, waits for a person to approve, and must undo the charge if the shipment later fails. A sleeping thread cannot do any of this across restarts.
steps.fix: A timer is just an event: 'fire at time T' is stored with the workflow, and a timer service queues a decision task when the time arrives. Nothing is held while it waits, so a million workflows can sleep for a month. A signal is an event appended from outside, such as an approval click or a carrier webhook, and it wakes the workflow, while a query reads its state without changing it. For failure, the workflow code is a saga: after each successful step it registers the matching compensation (refund, release stock), and when a later step fails for good it runs the registered compensations in reverse order. The compensations are activities too, so they are retried and idempotent.
steps.tradeoff: Waiting costs one row and a timer entry instead of a machine, and the undo logic sits in the same readable code as the steps. Compensations are not true rollbacks: an email that was sent stays sent, and in-between states are visible to other systems, so each compensation has to be designed with care.

steps.title: Shard histories by workflow id, and start a fresh history before one grows too long
steps.problem: Millions of workflows and tens of thousands of appends per second are too much for one database, and a workflow that loops for years would build a history too long to replay.
steps.fix: The workflow id is hashed to one of a fixed number of shards, for example 16,384, and each shard owns the histories, the timers and the task queue entries of its workflows. Shards are spread over database nodes, and one engine node holds a lease on a shard at a time, so appends to one workflow never race. Moving a shard between nodes changes the mapping and not the key. Every history is capped, in Temporal for example at 51,200 events or 50 MB, with warnings well before it. A long-running workflow ends by calling continue-as-new, which closes the current history and starts a new run with the same id, carrying over only the state it needs. Closed histories are archived after a retention period, and the live shards stay small.
steps.tradeoff: Load spreads evenly and replay time has a ceiling. A shard is still a hot spot for one very busy workflow, a cross-workflow query needs a separate search index, and continue-as-new code must pass its state forward on purpose.

steps.title: Version workflow code while instances are in flight
steps.problem: A workflow started in March may still be running in June. A new deploy that adds a step makes its replay decide differently from its recorded history, and the engine reports a non-determinism error.
steps.fix: There are two safe patterns. In the first, the code branches on a version marker: when it reaches the changed spot it asks the engine for a version, a new run records 'version 2', and an old replay finds no marker and takes the old branch. The second is worker versioning: each deploy is a build id, running workflows are pinned to the build that started them, and routing rules send new workflows to the new build while old builds stay up until their last workflow closes. Before shipping, a test replays real recorded histories of production workflows against the new code. A canary deploy of workers shows any replay failure on a small share first.
steps.tradeoff: In-flight workflows are never corrupted by a deploy, and old behaviour is kept exactly for those that need it. The code collects old branches, and pinned builds must be kept running for as long as the longest workflow, which can mean months.

failures.scenario: A workflow worker crashes in the middle of a decision
failures.impact: The in-memory state of the code is gone, and without care the workflow would stall or restart from the beginning.
failures.answer: Nothing was lost because the state is the history. The decision task times out, goes back on the queue, and another worker replays the events and continues. A worker that was only slow and returns late has its commands rejected, because it appends against an old history version.

failures.scenario: An activity charges the card, and then its worker dies before reporting
failures.impact: The engine cannot know whether the charge happened, so it retries and the customer may be charged twice.
failures.answer: The retry sends the same idempotency key, such as the workflow id with the step name. The payment provider recognises it and returns the original charge instead of creating a second one. Heartbeats shorten the time to notice a dead worker, and the retry policy adds backoff so the retries do not pile up.

failures.scenario: A deploy changes the order of steps while 50,000 orders are in flight
failures.impact: Replay of the old histories diverges from the new code and the affected workflows stop with a non-determinism error.
failures.answer: Branch on a version marker or pin old workflows to the old build. A replay test against recorded histories in CI would have caught it before the deploy, and a canary deploy limits the damage to a few workers. Fixing and redeploying lets the stuck workflows resume from where they were.

failures.scenario: The payment service is down for an hour
failures.impact: Every workflow at the charge step retries, and the retries themselves could keep the service from recovering.
failures.answer: Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, so the load falls off instead of staying constant. A circuit breaker and a rate limit on the activity task queue protect the dependency, and the workflows simply stay open until it returns. Their timeouts are long enough to cover an outage of this size, and a dashboard shows how many are waiting at that step.

failures.scenario: A history shard's database node fails
failures.impact: All workflows on that shard cannot make progress until their histories are readable again.
failures.answer: Each shard's data is replicated, and a replica is promoted. Appends are only acknowledged after they are durable, so nothing acknowledged is lost. Another engine node takes the shard lease, reloads its timers and task queue from the database, and the workflows continue. Affected workflows see a delay of seconds.

alternatives.title: How the process is executed

options.name: One script in one process
options.pro: The simplest thing, with no new infrastructure
options.con: A crash loses the state, a sleep holds a process, and a restart repeats steps

options.name: A persisted state machine, with no replay
options.pro: Survives crashes with one row per workflow, and is easy to query
options.con: The logic is split over states and transitions instead of being readable code, and an in-flight step can still run twice

options.name: Event-sourced history with deterministic replay
options.pro: Ordinary code, a full audit trail, and recovery on any worker
options.con: The code must be deterministic, a history can grow too long, and versioning needs care

alternatives.pick: Event-sourced replay for the general engine. A persisted state machine is enough for a short flow with a few states, and a script for jobs that can safely be started again.

alternatives.title: How workers get tasks

options.name: The engine pushes tasks to workers
options.pro: Low delay when a worker is known to be healthy
options.con: The engine has to track worker health and load, and it can push to a dead machine

options.name: Workers pull from task queues with a long poll
options.pro: Workers set their own pace and need no address, and a crashed worker simply stops asking
options.con: A poller holds a connection, and an idle queue still costs polls

alternatives.pick: Pull with a long poll. Add a sticky queue per worker so the next task of the same workflow goes to the worker that has it cached, with a fallback to the normal queue if that worker is slow.

alternatives.title: How to change code that is already running

options.name: Branch on a version marker in the code
options.pro: One deployment, and old and new instances share the workers
options.con: Old branches pile up in the code until the last old workflow closes

options.name: Pin each workflow to the build that started it
options.pro: No branching, and the old code runs exactly as before
options.con: Old builds must stay deployed and monitored for as long as the longest workflow

options.name: Wait for all workflows to finish before changing

alternatives.pick: Pin to a build for large changes, version markers for small ones, and replay-test recorded histories in every pipeline.

alternatives.title: Delivery guarantee for activities

options.name: At-most-once
options.con: A crash can leave the step undone with nobody noticing

options.name: At-least-once with idempotent activities
options.pro: Every step finishes, and a repeat has no extra effect
options.con: Every external call needs a key and a cooperating system

options.name: Distributed transaction across systems
options.con: Locks held across systems, and most payment APIs do not take part

alternatives.pick: At-least-once plus idempotency keys, because it is the only one that is both safe and realistic with external systems.
